title: Scientists have watched bacteria evolve in flasks every day since 1988
body: Since 24 February 1988, when Richard Lenski started twelve identical populations of E. coli, 1% of each flask has been moved daily into fresh medium. Samples are frozen every 500 generations as a **frozen fossil record** that can be thawed and raced against its own descendants: by 20,000 generations the bacteria grew about 70% faster than their ancestor. Between generations 31,000 and 31,500, one population learned to feed on citrate in the presence of oxygen, which E. coli normally cannot do. The experiment passed 80,000 generations in August 2024.

slides.heading: A day in the experiment, since 1988

steps.label: Twelve flasks of E. coli grow for a day
1% of each is moved into fresh medium
Every 500 generations, a sample is frozen

slides.question: How many generations had the bacteria reached by August 2024?
slides.explanation: The populations passed 80,000 generations in August 2024. At about 25 years per human generation, that would take people roughly two million years.

events.text: Started by Richard Lenski in California
One population found to eat citrate in air, a new trick
Moved to Jeffrey Barrick’s lab in Texas at 75,000 generations

slides.heading: Why freeze samples?
slides.text: Thawed ancestors can be grown side by side with their descendants, so fitness gains are measured directly rather than guessed. The frozen samples also let researchers go back and ask when the mutations behind the citrate trick first appeared.

slides.heading: The citrate surprise
slides.text: The growth medium has always contained citrate, which E. coli normally cannot grow on when oxygen is present. After more than 30,000 generations, population Ara-3 suddenly could, and its flask turned cloudy with new growth.

slides.clue: The compound one population learned to eat in the presence of oxygen, which E. coli normally cannot do
slides.detail: Citrate had been in the growth medium all along. Population Ara-3 learned to use it after more than 30,000 generations.
